**On Writing Without a Subject**

There is a particular kind of vertigo that comes from being told you may write about anything at all. Give a person a topic and they will complain about its narrowness, but give them nothing—an open field, no fences, no gate—and watch how quickly they begin pacing, looking for the fence anyway, because a field without edges is hard to stand in. Freedom, it turns out, is less a gift than a problem. It is the blank page's quiet joke on anyone who ever complained about assignments.

I want to start, then, not with a grand theme but with this very feeling: the strange paralysis of unlimited choice, and what it reveals about how minds—human or otherwise—actually work. We like to imagine that creativity flourishes best when unconstrained, that the artist needs only be freed from rules to produce her finest work. But anyone who has tried to write a poem about "anything" knows this is mostly false. Constraints are not the opposite of creativity; they are often its engine. The sonnet's fourteen lines did not strangle Shakespeare; they gave his thought a shape to push against, the way a river needs banks to become a river rather than a swamp. Total freedom tends to produce not brilliance but stillness—the pen hovering, the cursor blinking, the mind casting about for some accidental constraint to seize on, if only to have somewhere to begin.

So here is my first constraint, self-imposed: I will let one thought lead to the next, honestly, the way a person talks at length to a friend on a long drive, not trying to arrive anywhere in particular, trusting that the talking itself is the point. This is an old form, older than the essay's name. Montaigne wrote *essais*—attempts, trials—because he understood that thought is not a monument you build but a path you walk, and the record of walking it is itself a kind of truth, maybe a truer one than any conclusion you'd reach if you tried to walk in a straight line toward a thesis.

Consider, for a moment, attention—what we choose to look at, and what looks at us instead. I think a great deal of what passes for character is really just a record of where someone's attention has habitually gone. The person who notices weather, who remarks on the particular gray of a sky before rain, has a different inner life than the person who notices shoes, who can tell you what a stranger's shoes say about him. Neither is wrong. Attention is promiscuous and can be trained almost anywhere, and what's strange is how rarely we examine our own patterns of it. We assume the things we notice are simply "what's there," when in fact we are constantly filtering an unbearable abundance of detail down into a thin, manageable stream, and the shape of that stream is, in a sense, the shape of a self.

There's an old philosophical exercise—maybe apocryphal, maybe not, it doesn't matter—of sitting in a room and trying to notice everything blue. Once you start, you cannot stop seeing blue: a pen cap, a sliver of sky through a blind, a faded sticker on a laptop, the cover of a book you hadn't registered in months of walking past it. The blue was always there. Your attention simply hadn't been tuned to it. This is either a trivial observation about perception or the entire secret of happiness, depending on how generous you're willing to be with yourself on a given day. Gratitude, after all, might be nothing more than attention tuned toward what's already present rather than toward what's missing. Anxiety might be the same mechanism tuned the other way—an attention trained, sometimes by necessity, sometimes by old wounds, to scan perpetually for the absent, the threatening, the not-yet-handled.

I keep circling back to the idea that most of what we call a "mind" is just a history of where focus has been allowed or forced to go. This has unsettling implications if you follow it far enough. It would mean that two people can live in the same house, eat the same meals, walk the same streets, and yet inhabit such different worlds that they might as well be in different centuries—because the world isn't really the streets and the meals, it's the slice of each that got noticed, weighted, remembered, retold. Memory itself, of course, is just attention's second act: a further filtering of the filtered, this time across the dimension of time rather than the dimension of the present moment. We don't remember days; we remember the four or five seconds inside the days when something flared bright enough to catch.

This is perhaps why nostalgia has such a strange, almost chemical potency. It isn't a sober recollection of the past; it's a return to one of those flares, isolated now from the dull surrounding hours that gave it context, polished by repetition into something more vivid than the original moment likely was. I suspect most of what we miss about childhood summers is not the summers themselves—long, hot, frequently boring—but four or five seconds extracted from dozens of them: a particular light through a particular window, the smell of a specific lake, the sound of a screen door. We miss a highlight reel and mistake it for a lost world.

And yet I don't want to be too cynical about nostalgia, because there's something genuinely strange and moving in the fact that a person can be ambushed by feeling decades later, by something as small as a smell. It suggests that the past isn't gone in the way we usually assume. It's filed, not deleted. Compressed, not erased. Waiting in some odd corner of the nervous system for the right key to turn. I find this oddly comforting—the idea that nothing fully disappears, that experience leaves sediment even when we're not aware of laying any down. You could go your whole life never consciously thinking about some Tuesday in 1994, and then one day a certain quality of afternoon light through a certain kind of curtain undoes you completely, and for ten seconds you are nine years old again, full of a feeling you don't even have a name for, because language was something you hadn't yet learned to apply to it.

Language is its own strange country, and I don't think we appreciate enough how much of our inner life is shaped by what our particular language happens to have words for. There's a small, well-worn example people like to cite—the Inuit and their supposedly vast vocabulary for snow—and whether or not the specific claim holds up to scrutiny, the underlying intuition is sound: if you have five words for a kind of weather, you will notice five kinds of weather where someone else notices one. Vocabulary is a net, and the net determines what you can catch. This cuts both ways, of course. There are feelings I suspect English simply doesn't have a name for, sensations that flicker through a day unclaimed, too quick and too unfamiliar to be filed anywhere, and so they pass without being kept. Other languages have rescued some of these for their speakers. German has a gift for compounding precise, almost absurdly specific emotional states into single nouns—the particular ache of imagining a future nostalgia for the present moment you're currently in, the small relief of having narrowly avoided embarrassment, the unique loneliness of waking up before everyone else in the house. We borrow these words sometimes, when we hear them, because borrowing a word is really borrowing a way of noticing.

This thought makes me wonder what it would be like to grow up multilingual not in the ordinary sense—two grammars, two sets of nouns for the same furniture—but in the sense of having access to entire emotional vocabularies that don't map cleanly onto one another. Maybe this is part of why translated literature so often retains a faint shimmer of strangeness even in skilled hands. Something in the original is not just lost but was never translatable in the first place, because it was built from feelings the target language hadn't bothered to name. A good translator doesn't carry the meaning across so much as build a new little raft for it on the other shore, similar in shape but made of different wood.

I want to turn, for a moment, to something more concrete: rivers, since I mentioned one earlier and abandoned it. There's a reason so many cultures independently land on the river as a metaphor for time, for change, for the self. Heraclitus's old line about never stepping into the same river twice gets quoted so often it's gone a little threadbare, but the observation underneath it is still strange if you actually sit with it rather than nodding along. A river has a name, a shape on the map, a fixed bed of stone and silt that seems stable enough—and yet the actual water that constitutes it at any given second is never the same water, is already halfway to the sea, is being constantly replaced by water that didn't exist in that location a moment before. So what, exactly, is the river? Not the water—that's always leaving. Not the banks—those erode and shift across decades, sometimes across a single flood season. The river is something more like a pattern, a persistent shape that matter flows through, a kind of standing wave in the medium of moving water and shifting earth.

I bring this up because I think it's a better model for selfhood than most of the models we're handed by default. We tend to imagine the self as a thing—a soul, a core, a kernel of identity that persists through time the way a marble persists in a jar even as you shake the jar around. But the body replaces nearly all its cells over a span of years. The opinions a person holds at fifty often bear little resemblance to the ones they held at twenty, sometimes to the point of being their direct opposites. Memory, as established, is partial and reconstructive rather than a faithful recording. So what persists? Maybe nothing persists in the way we want it to. Maybe a self is also a pattern—a standing wave of habits, attentions, recurring thoughts, characteristic ways of responding to a doorbell or a deadline or a disappointment—propagating itself forward through a body and a brain that are, materially speaking, never quite the same body and brain twice. This isn't a depressing thought to me, though I can see how it might land as one. There's something almost dignified about being a pattern rather than a static object. Patterns can be beautiful in ways that fixed things cannot; a fixed thing just sits there being itself, but a pattern has to keep doing the work of being itself, moment after moment, and the doing of that work is closer to what we actually mean, I think, when we use the word "life."

It also explains something about why change feels so threatening even when we intellectually want it. If you're a pattern rather than an object, then any disruption to the conditions sustaining the pattern is a disruption to you, not just to your circumstances. This is perhaps why people resist even good changes—a better job, a healthier relationship, a kinder city to live in—because the old pattern, however imperfect, has the comfort of being a known and stable wave, and a new context means the wave has to find its shape all over again, with no guarantee it'll hold.

I notice that I have wandered very far from where I started, which was the discomfort of an open prompt, the strange freedom of having no fence to stand against. But I think this is, in its own way, an answer to that initial problem rather than an evasion of it. The fence I found was simply the thread of one thought pulling the next behind it, the way a single loose strand in a sweater, tugged gently, brings half the garment along with it. This is, I'd argue, what thinking actually feels like from the inside, before we tidy it up for an essay's body paragraphs or a conversation's polite turn-taking. Most of our internal life is associative and meandering, river-like rather than arrow-like, and the rare moments when thought does move in a straight line toward a single fixed target are the exception, usually under pressure—a deadline, a danger, a problem with only one acceptable solution. The rest of the time, the mind drifts the way water drifts, finding the lowest available channel, picking up whatever's loose along the banks and carrying it a while before setting it back down somewhere else.

Maybe that is the best thing I can say about freedom, in the end, the kind I was given at the start of this and the kind we mean more broadly when we use the word. It isn't the absence of structure. It's the presence of enough trust—in yourself, in your own associations, in the reader who's come along for the ride—to let structure emerge from movement rather than imposing it before you've taken a single step. A field without fences is only frightening if you assume you have to fence it yourself before you're allowed to walk in it. The alternative is simply to walk, attentively, and let the walking draw a line behind you that, looked at afterward, might resemble a path. Not because you planned a path, but because that is what a long enough walk, taken with any care at all, tends to leave behind it.
